## Infrared Thermography for Electrical Systems

### Thermal Imaging Camera Basics and Emissivity
When you pull out a FLIR T540 or a Fluke Ti480 PRO, you aren't just taking a picture; you are measuring the infrared radiation emitted by an object. The most critical setting on your camera before you even point it at a panel is emissivity ($\epsilon$). Emissivity is the measure of an object's ability to emit infrared energy. It ranges from 0.00 (a perfect mirror) to 1.00 (a perfect blackbody). 

If you are scanning a heavily oxidized copper busbar, the emissivity might be around 0.60 to 0.70. However, if you are looking at a brand-new, shiny copper or aluminum lug, the emissivity can drop below 0.10. If you leave your camera set to the default 0.95 (typical for electrical tape or painted surfaces) while scanning bare metal, your camera will read the reflected temperature of the surrounding environment instead of the actual temperature of the lug. 

> **CRITICAL:** Never trust a temperature reading on shiny, unpainted metal. If you need an accurate reading on a bare aluminum lug, apply a piece of standard black electrical tape (emissivity ~0.95) to the lug while the circuit is de-energized, re-energize, and scan the tape.

### Identifying Electrical Connection Hot Spots
The primary use of thermography in a plant is finding high-resistance connections before they fail. A loose connection, corrosion, or improper crimping increases resistance. According to Ohm's Law ($P = I^2R$), as resistance increases, the power dissipated as heat increases exponentially with the current.
